title: Household spending expectations rise while credit access, financial outlook, and job-finding confidence deteriorate
source_unit: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Center for Microeconomic Data, August 2026 Survey of Consumer Expectations, released 8 September 2026
geography: United States; nationally representative internet-based rotating panel of approximately 1,300 household heads, fielded 3–31 August 2026

observations.period: August 2026; spending expectations and household financial outlook

denominator.unit: approximately 1,300 household heads in the nationally representative rotating panel

spending_growth.unit: median percent expected one-year-ahead household spending growth

income_growth.unit: median percent expected one-year-ahead household income growth

financial_outlook.value: Perceptions and expectations about household financial situations deteriorated, with more respondents reporting or expecting a worse situation

spending_constraint_gap.value: Expected spending growth can exceed expected income growth even as perceived household financial security worsens

observations.method: New York Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations, a nationally representative internet-based rotating panel of approximately 1,300 household heads; respondents participate for up to 12 months.
observations.uncertainty: Expectations are not realized spending or income, and the release does not identify whether expected spending reflects necessities, prices, substitution, or volume changes.
observations.subgroup: U.S. household heads, with expectations available by age, geography, income, education, and numeracy.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher spending growth may largely reflect expected price increases or essential outlays rather than stronger discretionary consumption; deteriorating financial perceptions can coexist with planned spending.

observations.period: August 2026; credit access and short-run debt-payment risk

denominator.unit: approximately 1,300 household heads in the SCE panel

credit_access.value: The net share reporting that credit is harder to obtain increased, and future credit availability expectations deteriorated

missed_payment_risk.unit: mean perceived probability of missing a minimum debt payment in the next three months

credit_buffer.value: The ability to use credit as a household buffer is perceived to be narrowing at the same time that spending expectations remain elevated

observations.method: SCE household-finance questions on perceived credit access and probability of missing a minimum debt payment.
observations.uncertainty: The missed-payment probability is a subjective expectation, not observed delinquency; the release does not show which debt types or households drive the movement.
observations.subgroup: Household heads with differing credit access, debt obligations, income, and financial buffers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Credit tightening perceptions may reflect normalization from unusually easy access or changes in demand; a higher perceived risk need not translate into missed payments.

observations.period: August 2026; unemployment risk and job-finding confidence

denominator.unit: approximately 1,300 household heads in the SCE panel

higher_unemployment.unit: mean perceived probability that the U.S. unemployment rate will be higher in one year

job_finding.unit: mean perceived probability of finding a job if current job were lost

job_loss.unit: mean perceived probability of losing one's job in the next 12 months

labor_security_split.value: People perceive a weaker labor-market environment while their own expected job loss declines somewhat, separating macro fear from individual positioning

observations.method: SCE labor-market expectation questions, with reported changes across age, education, and income groups.
observations.uncertainty: These are subjective probabilities and do not forecast actual unemployment, job loss, or re-employment; individual and macro expectations can move differently.
observations.subgroup: Household heads across age, education, income, and employment categories; changes in job-loss and quit expectations were driven especially by lower-education and under-$100,000-income respondents.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower expected personal job loss alongside worse macro expectations may indicate labor-market compositional change, precautionary belief, or confidence in one's own employability rather than general security.

observations.period: August 2026; price-category exposure and inflation uncertainty

denominator.unit: approximately 1,300 household heads in the SCE panel

gas_price_expectation.unit: median percent expected year-ahead gas-price change

food_price_expectation.unit: median percent expected year-ahead food-price change

medical_price_expectation.unit: median percent expected year-ahead medical-care price change

rent_expectation.unit: median percent expected year-ahead rent change

category_exposure.value: Household inflation experience is composed of salient categories with different necessity and substitution profiles, not only an aggregate inflation expectation

observations.method: SCE category-specific price-expectation questions covering gas, food, medical care, college education, and rent.
observations.uncertainty: Expected category inflation is not realized price change and may reflect attention, recent experience, or local exposure; category medians do not show household-level budget incidence.
observations.subgroup: Households with differing spending baskets, rent exposure, health-care needs, education costs, and transportation dependence.
observations.counterinterpretation: High medical or rent expectations may be concentrated among households with particular contracts or needs; substitution and fixed-price arrangements can alter lived impact.

related_sources.claim: New York Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations series and methodology context.
Official release for the August 2026 SCE findings.

boundary: This record adds a household-finance route from category-specific price and labor expectations through income-spending divergence, credit access, missed-payment risk, and unequal financial buffers. It does not establish realized inflation, delinquency, unemployment, consumption volume, or causal effects of monetary or credit conditions.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official New York Fed release reviewed for field dates, rotating-panel frame, spending and income expectations, credit access, missed-payment risk, labor expectations, category-specific prices, and subgroup notes.
